Muck Boots

10 Brands

If you are in a dry to moderately rainy climate they probably do not make much sense. However if you have a lot of rain or snow, these are great. They don't replace your regular boots but are used as an offset to them especially when really wet out or in snow .

I picked up a set of farm boots years back similar to the Ranger ones. Having used them 3 winters now, they are my go-to for outside work. Not tried hiking in them but suspect some might be OK for short hikes if on snowpack or mud. Would not try them on dry ground though.

I added thick felt insoles to insulate my feet from the sole. Cold will transmit right up otherwise. I used thick felt ones (ebay/Russia/cheap) which worked fine. I may buy sheepskin ones this year to try. You also need heavy wool socks with a lot of "loft" to keep an insulating barrier between your calf and the boot. Doing this I've been on snowpack in sub-20° weather for hours without issue.

Because the boots are essentially one piece, heat from your foot is trapped. I've never had an issue with perspiration building up or my feet becoming wet. I surmise that thick socks allow perspiration to vent away, up, & out. My feet stayed toasty. Anyways, something you might want to consider adding to your kit.

I've bought & sold many Goodyear brand waders & boots from the 1960s. Although they may have developed some surface cracks, they do not go all the way through and the rubber has remained pliable with the boots leak-free. That speaks to high process quality and use of quality materials to survive that long. I would confine my choices to new boots of known good reputation & feedback in this regard.

I buy a couple sets of Chinese made "rubber" garden gloves every season. Construction is a rubber-like substance over cloth. Quite pliable and comfortable to wear. They provide great service for ~6-8 months then they fail. Usually what happens is they develop cracks and then the material begins to flake off at flex points. They can go from looking fine to falling apart in an hour of use. The other thing that happens is if left undisturbed long enough the covering breaks down on its own. This maybe unfair to compare cheap Chinese rubber gloves to cheap Chinese rubber boots but it is worth noting.

I bought a couple sets of gloves but one pair fell behind bag of plant fertilizer I seldom used. I found them the beginning of this year and they'd probably been hidden & still stapled together for ~2+ years. They were both stuck to the bag as well as each other and were rock hard. Now it is quite likely there are good quality Chinese rubber boots out there, how would you know? Finding out they aren't good after SHTF would suck. The farm boots I bought were French made but there are also greatUS, Canadian, English, Irish, and German ones out there.

Shop around.

Of course, YMMV!

reupholstering furniture isnt that difficult.

start at the bottom of the peice removing the staples or tacks. (if you encounter horsehair, hog hair keep it, it's valuable.) then usually the back will be removed before the outside-sides. the fabric can be kept and used to size the new peices of fabrics. ive seen fine upholsters use pins to judge sizing by placing the new fabric cuts where they go.

the white felty stuff under the fabric can be left on the furniture. the 'interior fabric/underneath the cushions' is removed via access to the outsidesides of the peice; after removing the outsideside fabric you will see where the 'interior fabric/underneath the cusions' is stapled in place and so there it will be de-stapled.

by the way,,, the ''proper way'' to use a staple remover is often by laying it on it's side rather than flat(with two claws on the wood) and then getting a claw under the staple and rolling the stapleremover as so lever the staple out with torsinal force. sharp/non flat ends is ideal. but whatever removes the staple the best.

there's tutorials on it. my grandmother and mom have done peices. you can use a glue gun to speed the process. a heavy duty stapler (ideally air powered) is best. for hardwoods use pointed staples.

if you go to an upholster buy the fabric yourself or ask them what they already have on-hand for a discount price. often you may find outsourcing of the work which you might be able to work directly with.
